facts.claim: "Battery" is track 10 of the 21-track album "I'm fine" by TOKYO CHILL LAB. It runs 3:04.
"Battery" was released on November 22, 2025 on the TOKYO CHILL LAB label, as part of the album "I'm Fine".
Shazam credits TOKYO CHILL LAB with vocals, composition, lyrics and production on "Battery". It lists Keisuke.T as co-producer.
The Linkcore credits list TOKYO CHILL LAB for lyrics, composition, production, vocals and programming on "Battery". They list Keisuke.T as co-producer.
The YouTube release lists TOKYO CHILL LAB as both lyricist and composer, with a ℗ 2025 TOKYO CHILL LAB notice.
Shazam lists "Battery" under the Hip-Hop/Rap genre.
On Spotify, "Battery" had over 1 million plays, far more than the album's title track at about 220,000. This was the figure when the page was indexed.
"Battery" reached No. 34 on the iTunes Store Hip-Hop/Rap top songs chart in Thailand on 24 May 2026.
The Soul Over AI directory lists TOKYO CHILL LAB as an anonymous, high-output project. It says the YouTube bio describes all tracks and visuals as original creations produced using AI.
The Soul Over AI directory says the project releases albums roughly every two weeks. It says no identifiable information about the artist exists beyond Spotify and YouTube.

research.lineage: A Tokyo-branded, anonymous, high-output project, described as AI-assisted, that releases mood-driven bilingual English and Japanese tracks. Its albums are released frequently, and streaming platforms file "Battery" under hip-hop/rap.

draft:
The voice on **Battery** starts in English and slides into Japanese without changing its temperature. It stays breathy and close, a little low in spirit, like it's saving its energy. Underneath, a clean electric guitar picks out arpeggios through a soft delay, a bass walks in small steps, and a drum machine holds a mid-tempo beat with a light swing. Nothing lifts. Nothing drops away. The arrangement holds its shape, and that steadiness is the song's whole argument.

The titles do some of the talking. A battery runs down quietly, and the album it sits on is called "I'm fine," the phrase people reach for when they'd rather not explain. As track 10 of 21, "Battery" never gets louder than that pairing. The melancholy isn't in a big chorus or a vocal break. It's in the restraint: a voice that never pushes, a groove that won't build toward relief. It sounds like getting through the day on whatever charge is left, and not bringing it up.

The production is dry and polished, every part set apart with room around it, so the delay trailing off the guitar is the one thing in the mix that lingers. Streaming services file the song under hip-hop/rap, and the patient drum machine bears that out. But the feel sits closer to late-night chill beats, loops built for company rather than confrontation. The switch between languages is the one real turn, and it works less as a hook than as a change of register. The same mood comes through twice, in two languages, at the same low volume.

Worth knowing: TOKYO CHILL LAB is an anonymous, high-output project that puts out albums roughly every two weeks, and its YouTube bio describes its tracks and visuals as made using AI. The project is credited with the writing, vocals and production, with Keisuke.T as co-producer. That raises a fair question about whose tiredness this is, since no person has stepped forward to claim it. Listeners found something in it anyway. "Battery" passed a million Spotify plays, several times the album's title track, and reached No. 34 on Thailand's iTunes hip-hop/rap chart. The feeling may be general by design, which is also why it fits so many people's low evenings.

It sticks because it doesn't ask you to feel better, only to keep it company while you run low.
